Thank you for submitting your article "Regenerative neurogenic response from glia requires insulin driven neuron-glia communication" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Utpal Banerjee as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Hongyan Wang (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

As the editors have judged that your manuscript is of interest, but as described below that additional experiments are required before it is published, we would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). First, because many researchers have temporarily lost access to the labs, we will give authors as much time as they need to submit revised manuscripts. We are also offering, if you choose, to post the manuscript to bioRxiv (if it is not already there) along with this decision letter and a formal designation that the manuscript is "in revision at eLife". Please let us know if you would like to pursue this option. (If your work is more suitable for medRxiv, you will need to post the preprint yourself, as the mechanisms for us to do so are still in development.)

The reviewers feel that while many comments were adequately addressed, several essential points remain problematic and do not support the conclusions of the manuscript. These include experiments with technical difficulties or uninterpretable results. If you are willing and able to address the reviewers' concerns you may resubmit a revised manuscript with a detailed rebuttal letter.

It is required that you address the following to be reconsidered for publication:

1) Additional NSC markers must be optimized. Dpn staining in some figures is unconvincing and must be verified using additional markers.

2) Cell markers routinely used by many labs must work (Wor, Ase, Elav)

3) Dpn is a reagent that works well and should be clear.

Please note that this decision letter does not guarantee that this manuscript will be accepted. At least one reviewer feels that their concerns were not addressed in the revised manuscript and that it is in everyone's best interest that the authors can prove that the inability to provide the appropriate expression patterns is not indicative of a deeper problem with the underlying hypothesis.

1) The main conclusion of the paper (glia transform into NSCs which produce neurons) but is not supported by data: only one NSC marker used out of many available.

The authors tried two additional NSC markers but did not observe staining, despite these reagents working for many labs in many publications. "We did not consider these results satisfactory enough to present."

This is a major flaw, especially how unusual the Dpn staining looks like in the ectopic Dpn+ cells (very speckly). Failure to show additional NSC markers very concerning is a real issue; also no evidence for asymmetric cell division at mitosis (a hallmark of these NSCs).

2) There is no evidence for proliferation of the ectopic Dpn+ cells. The authors state that ectopic Dpn+ cells expressed the S phase marker PCNA:GFP and can be labeled with the mitotic marker pH3.

However, only panes 8A-C show PCNA+ Dpn+ cells, which are increased following dilp-6 overexpression. No data in the figure shows ectopic Dpn+ cells that are pH3. The rest of the figure shows glial markers and PCNA or pH3, which is irrelevant to the question of whether ectopic Dpn+ cells can divide.

3) To show evidence that ectopic Dpn+ cells produce neuronal progeny, the authors used the pros-Gal4 line to drive flybow expression, and observed a small cluster of cells that included one Dpn+ and one Elav+ cell. As the authors say "this does not prove these cells are related by lineage, but is consistent with it."

This does not show Dpn+ cells are producing neurons.

4) The authors also used "flip out" genetics to permanently mark glial cells.

The genetics shown in the figure, legend, and reviewer response will not specifically label glia. The genotype is: actGAL4>y+>UASGFP/UAS-FLP; repoGAL4/Dilp-6. This would induce Flp widely, in all cells due to ubiquitous expression of actin-gal4. Most likely, the authors wrote down the wrong genotype in the figure, legend, Materials and methods, and reviewer response – it is probably actin promotor-FRT-stop-FRT-GFP. They cite Table 1 for more information on genotypes but there is no Table 1 provided.

5) In order to call kon and ia-2 partners, a direct physical interaction should be shown. The authors could not get the biochemical experiments to work for various reasons. Changed text from "partners" to "functional neuronal partner."

The continued use of “partner” is inappropriate. The most accurate description of their relationship is that they show “genetic interactions” – so the first results header should be changed from "Ia-2 is a functional partner of Kon" to "Ia-2 and kon show genetic interactions."

6) Saying ectopic Pros+ cells are GMCs or neurons is premature and can be definitively resolved by staining for Wor or Dpn (neuroblast-specific), Ase (neuroblast and GMC), and Elav (neurons). All have been extensively used by many labs. The authors could not get the stains to work.

This is unsatisfactory.

7) The text says loss of ia-2 "destabilizes cell fate" – which is a vague term that obscures the phenotype. The authors changed text to "… upregulated GMC and NSC markers."

They looked at Dpn but no other NSC marker, and Pros is not a specific GMC marker, also being expressed in neuropile glia near the midline (which is worrying).

8) Dpn staining in Figure 3D is unconvincing; everything looks speckly. The authors state that Dpn staining is speckly in their hands.

Many labs have used Dpn to mark neuroblasts, it is a very reliable reagent. The authors have good Dpn staining in other figures; this suggest to me that the ectopic Dpn+ cells are different from the normal Dpn+ NPCs, leading to different protein localization/levels. This concern is reinforced by the failure of the authors to show the ectopic Dpn+ cells express any other NSC marker.

9) Ectopic Dpn+ cells were not quantified due to due to the disruption and variability of the abdominal crush procedure. The authors only counted the VNCs in which they could see ectopic Dpn+ (cells).

Cherry-picking only VNCs that show ectopic Dpn+ cells is inappropriate.

10) In response to InR-Gal4 expression concerns, the authors state "we do not know whether (InR-gal4) represents the endogenous expression pattern". It labels sparse patterns of neurons and sporadic glial cells.

The authors directly state in the revised manuscript "we visualized InR expression using available GAL4 lines to drive his-YFP" but in the reviewer response they acknowledge this is not accurate.

results.result: Ia-2 is expressed exclusively in neurons and genetically interacts with Kon. Kon loss of function in glia increases ia-2 mRNA levels approximately threefold, while Kon overexpression in neurons or glia decreases ia-2 mRNA by 25%. Ia-2 overexpression in glia decreases kon mRNA levels. RNAi knock-down of ia-2 in neurons reduces ia-2 transcripts to 20% of wild-type levels, while knock-down in glia has no effect. Immunostaining shows Ia-2YFP+ cells are Elav+ (neuronal marker) but lack Repo (glial marker) and Dpn (neuroblast marker).
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C115 provide converging qRT-PCR evidence demonstrating mutual regulation between kon and ia-2, with appropriate controls and multiple RNAi lines. Claims C116-C120 provide immunostaining evidence confirming neuronal-specific expression of Ia-2. The genetic interaction is well-supported by multiple independent experimental approaches with consistent results.

results.result: Ia-2 expression is regulated by Notch and Prospero (Pros). Notch loss of function increases ia-2 mRNA levels approximately twofold, while NotchICD overexpression in glia has no significant effect. Pros overexpression in glia increases ia-2 mRNA levels by twofold. Pros is a transcription factor expressed in glia, neuroblasts, GMCs, and some neurons, suggesting it could directly regulate ia-2 expression in multiple cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 provide qRT-PCR data showing regulation of ia-2 by Notch and Pros. The inference that Pros could directly regulate ia-2 (C107) is reasonable given the stronger effect of Pros GOF compared to LOF. The data support that ia-2 participates in the kon-Notch-pros regenerative gene network (C110).

results.result: Kon loss of function in glia increases the number of Ia-2YFP+ cells along the midline. These ectopic cells are neurons (Elav+ Repo−). Kon overexpression in neurons or glia does not affect Ia-2YFP+ midline cell numbers. The increase in neurons with kon loss of function could explain the increased ia-2 mRNA levels observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 provide imaging and quantification data showing increased Ia-2YFP+ cells with kon LOF. Claim C123 confirms these are neurons through marker analysis. The conclusion that Kon and Ia-2 are mutually exclusive in glia and neurons (C130) is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experiments.

results.result: Loss of ia-2 function increases the number of small Pros+ cells that are neurons (Elav+ Repo−), potentially including GMCs. Genetic inference suggests ia-2 represses pros. Pros is normally found in nuclei of some neurons, glia, and all GMCs. In neuroblasts, Pros is cytoplasmic, and nuclear translocation drives the switch from neuroblast to GMC fate. Pros represses Dpn, the general neural stem cell marker.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C133 provide imaging data showing increased small Pros+ Elav+ Repo− cells with ia-2 LOF. The genetic inference that ia-2 represses pros (C135) is reasonable based on the LOF phenotype. Claims C136-C139 provide established knowledge about Pros function, supporting the interpretation of the results.

results.result: Both ia-2 gain and loss of function increase the total number of abdominal VNC Dpn+ cells. Supernumerary Dpn+ cells are located at ectopic positions along the midline and around the neuropile, distinct from normal developmental neuroblasts. These cells were visualized at 120 hr AEL after developmental neuroblasts disappear, and Dpn levels in ectopic cells are lower than in thoracic neuroblasts. The effect is non-autonomous, suggesting communication between neurons and glia induces an ectopic neural stem cell state.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C144 provide imaging and quantification data showing ectopic Dpn+ cells with both ia-2 GOF and LOF, using multiple RNAi lines. The spatial and temporal characterization distinguishes these from developmental neuroblasts. The inference of non-autonomous signaling (C147-C148) is reasonable given that neurons themselves appear unaffected.

results.result: CNS injury increases ia-2 mRNA levels approximately twofold at 5-7 hr post-injury, recovering by 24 hr, paralleling the effect on kon expression. Injury induces ectopic abdominal Dpn+ cells that are distinct from developmental neuroblasts, located in dorsal positions and surrounding the neuropile. The number of ectopic Dpn+ cells increases significantly in injured samples, with incidence decreasing as larval age at injury increases. Most ectopic Dpn+ cells lack Ia-2YFP.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C152 provide qRT-PCR data showing injury-induced ia-2 upregulation. Claims C153-C163 provide extensive imaging and quantification data from multiple injury time points, demonstrating injury-induced ectopic neural stem cells. The spatial and temporal characterization is thorough. The inference that ia-2 is responsible for injury-induced Dpn+ cells (C164) is reasonable but correlative.

results.result: Ia-2 functions in dense core vesicles to release insulin and neurotransmitters. There are eight Drosophila insulin-like peptides (Dilps), and Ia-2 affects only Dilp-6. Dilp-6 is expressed in cortex and blood-brain barrier CNS glia and activates neural stem cell proliferation following quiescence in normal development. Most dilp-6 expressing cells in the abdominal larval VNC are cortex and surface glia (Repo+ Pros−), with some neurons (Repo− Elav+).
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C169 cite established knowledge about Ia-2 and Dilp-6 function. Claims C170-C172 provide imaging data characterizing dilp-6 expression pattern using a GAL4 reporter, confirming expression in cortex/surface glia and some neurons. The data are consistent with prior work.

results.result: Kon knock-down in glia significantly reduces dilp-6 mRNA levels, indicating dilp-6 expression depends on kon in glia. InR is expressed in both neurons and glia. In third instar larvae, Dilp-6 is produced and secreted by Ia-2 from some neurons, mostly produced in non-neuropile glia, and received by InR in neurons and glia including neuropile glia.
results.evaluation: Claim C173 provides qRT-PCR data showing kon-dependent dilp-6 expression. Claim C175 is supported by imaging data and single-cell RNAseq confirmation. Claims C176-C178 integrate multiple findings to describe the Dilp-6 signaling circuit, though some aspects are inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: A neuron-glia communication loop amplifies Dilp-6, with Kon as a limiting step. KonICD is distributed in both cytoplasm and nucleus of glial cells, where it could regulate gene expression. Overexpression of konICD in glia increases glial cell number, demonstrating KonICD can induce glial proliferation. Full-length Kon is normally cleaved, releasing KonICD to promote glial proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C188 provide imaging data showing nuclear and cytoplasmic localization of HA-tagged KonICD. Claims C189-C190 provide quantification data showing konICD overexpression increases glial cell number. The inference that full-length Kon is cleaved (C191) is reasonable given that both full-length Kon and KonICD induce proliferation.

results.result: Dilp-6 overexpression in glia increases glial cell number comparably to KonICD, and this is rescued by concomitant InRDN overexpression, demonstrating Dilp-6 activates InR signaling in glia to induce proliferation. Kon is not required for neural stem cell development. InR signaling can activate Kon cleavage downstream in glia. A non-autonomous relay from neuronal Ia-2 to glial Kon promotes glial proliferation and induces a positive feedback loop amplifying Dilp-6 production from glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C194 provide epistasis data demonstrating Dilp-6 acts through InR in glia. Claims C195-C196 show Kon is not required in neuroblasts. The inference that InR activates Kon cleavage (C197) is reasonable based on the epistasis experiments. Claim C201 integrates multiple findings into a coherent model supported by the data.

results.result: Overexpression of InRDN with dilp-6 in glia reduces Dpn levels in thoracic neuroblasts. Overexpression of kon-full-length or konICD in glia does not induce ectopic abdominal Dpn+ cells. konICD overexpression does not significantly alter mRNA levels for dilp-6 or dpn, indicating KonICD does not directly function as a transcription factor. Kon likely regulates dilp-6 indirectly by influencing glial cell fate and does not induce ectopic Dpn+ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C202-C205 provide imaging and qRT-PCR data showing Kon/KonICD overexpression does not induce Dpn+ cells or alter gene expression. The conclusion that KonICD does not function as a transcription factor (C206) is supported by the qRT-PCR data. The inference about indirect regulation (C209) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Overexpression of ia-2 induces ectopic abdominal Dpn+ cells along the midline and surrounding the neuropile. Dilp-6 overexpression has a stronger effect. Both Ia-2 and Dilp-6 can induce dpn expression, potentially in glia, but Kon alone cannot, indicating insulin signaling is required. Epistasis experiments demonstrate Ia-2 induces ectopic neural stem cells via Dilp-6 and InR signaling in glia, and ectopic Dpn+ cells originate from glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C211-C214 provide imaging and quantification data showing ia-2 and dilp-6 induce Dpn+ cells. Claims C217-C223 provide comprehensive epistasis analysis demonstrating the pathway: ia-2 → Dilp-6 → InR in glia → Dpn+ cells. Multiple rescue experiments with dilp-6 RNAi, kon RNAi, and InRDN provide strong support for the proposed pathway.

results.result: Dilp-6 overexpression induces Dpn expression in two distinct glial populations: lateral/dorsal Repo+ cells around the neuropile (neuropile glia/'astrocytes') and midline Wrp+ cells (midline glia). G-TRACE lineage tracing demonstrates ectopic Dpn+ cells originate from glial cells. The presence of both GFP and RFP in G-TRACE+ Dpn+ cells suggests glial cell fate has not been suppressed and cells may be in the process of reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Claims C226-C229 provide imaging data characterizing two distinct populations of ectopic Dpn+ cells using glial subtype markers. Claims C230-C233 provide G-TRACE lineage tracing data demonstrating glial origin. The interpretation about reprogramming (C233) is reasonable based on the presence of both GFP and RFP markers.

results.result: Dilp-6 overexpression results in ectopic Dpn+ PCNA-GFP+ cells in lateral positions around the neuropile and along the midline, indicating these cells are in S-phase. Dilp-6 induces proliferation of both Repo+ glia and Wrp+ midline glia. Some dividing PCNA-GFP+ Wrp+ cells also express Dpn, and ia-2 overexpression induces proliferation of Wrp+ Dpn+ cells (pH3+), demonstrating that glial-derived Dpn+ cells can divide.
results.evaluation: Claims C235-C240 provide imaging and quantification data showing Dilp-6-induced proliferation using PCNA-GFP. Claims C241-C244 demonstrate that Dpn+ cells of glial origin can divide using both PCNA-GFP and pH3 markers. The data provide strong evidence for proliferation of reprogrammed glial cells.

results.result: Dilp-6 overexpression with pros-GAL4 results in groups of GFP+ cells comprising a GFP+ cell, a GFP+Dpn+Elav− cell, and a GFP+Dpn−Elav+ cell, consistent with reprogrammed glia becoming neurogenic. Lineage tracing shows ectopic Dpn+ cells originate from glia and can produce neurons, as evidenced by GFP+Elav+ cells near ectopic Dpn+ cells. However, neurogenesis is limited, with only small cell clusters observed. This may be due to limited time before pupariation or insufficient factors for complete neurogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C245-C251 provide lineage tracing data demonstrating glial-derived Dpn+ cells can produce neurons. The observation of small clusters (C252) and the speculations about limiting factors (C253-C257) are reasonable interpretations. The evidence for neurogenesis is present but limited in extent, as acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: A novel molecular mechanism involving Kon/NG2 and insulin signaling drives regenerative neurogenic response from glia. Ia-2 induces initial Dilp-6 secretion from neurons, which is received by glia. A positive feedback loop amplifies Kon-dependent Dilp-6 production by cortex glia, which is then relayed to neuropile glia, resulting in in vivo reprogramming of glial cells into neural stem cells. This mechanism can induce both glial regeneration and neural stem cells from glia, potentially also neurons. The process is stochastic with variable penetrance, but all glia convert when activated Ras or PI3K are combined with Dilp-6. This mechanism may operate in mammals, as Ia-2, NG2/Kon, and insulin signaling have conserved functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C263-C267 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model supported by extensive experimental data. Claims C268-C269 acknowledge the stochastic nature and the importance of insulin signaling levels. Claims C270-C275 discuss evolutionary conservation based on cited literature. The model is well-supported by the data, though the extent of neurogenesis is limited.

results.result: Dpn is mostly induced in neuropile-associated glial cells, suggesting neuropile glia have neurogenic potential. Drosophila 'astrocytes' and midline glia express Notch, pros, kon, and InR, and share features with mammalian NG2-glia. In mammals, the combination of Notch1, Prox1, and NG2 is unique to NG2-glia. Notch and insulin signaling positively regulate dpn expression. The data indicate Notch-Kon/NG2-insulin synergy triggers dpn expression activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C276-C281 provide observations and speculations about which glial subtypes have neurogenic potential, supported by the data showing dpn induction primarily in neuropile glia. Claims C282-C289 integrate findings with cited literature to propose a mechanism involving Notch-Kon-insulin synergy. The synthesis is reasonable and supported by the data and prior work.

results.result: Upon injury, Notch, Pros, Kon/NG2, Ia-2, and insulin signaling function together to enable regenerative production of both glial cells and neural stem cells from glia. Induced neural stem cells may generate glia from daughter cells that inherit Kon or neurons from daughter cells that lack Kon but have Pros. Developmental neural stem cells are thought to be eliminated through Pros upregulation and terminal differentiation into glia, but these findings imply such termination may not be final. A neuron-glia communication relay involving Ia-2, Dilp-6, Kon, and InR is responsible for induction of neural stem cells from glia, their proliferation, and limited neurogenesis. Neuronal Ia-2 and Dilp-6 trigger two distinct responses in glia: in cortex glia, insulin signaling boosts Kon-dependent Dilp-6 amplification and glial regeneration; in neuropile NG2-like glia, insulin signaling induces neural stem cell fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C290-C297 synthesize the major findings and implications of the study. The model of distinct responses in different glial subtypes (C296) is well-supported by the data. The speculation about asymmetric cell division (C290-C291) is reasonable but not directly tested. The implication about developmental neural stem cell termination (C293-C294) is an interesting inference from the findings.

results.result: A genetic screen exploiting the kon overexpression VNC elongation phenotype identified genes that interact with kon. Knock-down of known interactors (integrins, Notch signaling factors, secretases, phosphatases) rescued the phenotype, validating the approach. Knock-down of phosphatases ptp99A, ptp69D, ptp4E, and most prominently lar (a negative regulator of insulin signaling) from neurons rescued the phenotype. Knock-down of Akt and ia-2 also caused some rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 describe the screening approach and validation with known interactors. Claims C89-C92 report the identification of insulin signaling-related genes, particularly lar and ia-2. The screening approach is sound and the validation with known interactors supports the reliability of the method. However, the authors acknowledge that multiple genes can affect VNC length, so rescue phenotypes may not necessarily reflect specific interactions.

results.result: Background and motivation for the study: Understanding injury-induced neurogenesis in animals could help promote regeneration in humans. Regenerative neurogenesis may originate from glia, and NG2 may sense injury-induced neuronal signals, but these are unknown. The CNS can regenerate in some animals through de novo neurogenesis. Regenerative neurogenesis may reflect an evolutionarily conserved mechanism, making Drosophila a suitable model. NG2-glia are progenitor cells in the adult human brain that can produce neurons postnatally and upon injury. NG2 is a transmembrane protein that can be cleaved to release an intracellular domain that regulates gene expression. Key partners of NG2 produced from neurons remain largely unknown.
results.evaluation: These claims provide background knowledge and motivation for the study, supported by citations to prior work. They establish the scientific context and rationale for investigating NG2/Kon and its neuronal partners in regenerative neurogenesis. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Background on Kon/NG2 in Drosophila: Kon is the Drosophila NG2 homologue that functions in glia to promote glial proliferation, cell fate determination, and CNS injury repair. Kon works with Notch and Prospero in a homeostatic gene network that drives glial regeneration upon injury. Injury induces Notch-dependent upregulation of kon in glia. The relationship between Notch, Kon, and Pros is conserved in mice. Kon is the key driver of the glial regenerative response to CNS injury. The authors observed that injury results in incomplete neuropile repair, suggesting injury might induce neuronal events.
results.evaluation: These claims provide background on prior work on Kon/NG2 in Drosophila and mammals, supported by citations. They establish the foundation for the current study's investigation of neuronal partners of Kon. The observation about incomplete neuropile repair (C80) motivates the hypothesis that neuronal factors interact with Kon.

results.result: Discussion of injury-induced cues for neuronal differentiation: In mammals, injury creates a distinct cellular environment that prompts glial cells to generate different cell types. Elevated Sox-2 can reprogramme NG2-glia into neurons, but only upon injury. During normal development, NG2-glia may only produce oligodendrocyte lineage cells, but upon injury they can also produce astrocytes and neurons. This suggests there are injury-induced cues for neuronal differentiation.
results.evaluation: These claims discuss prior work on injury-induced neuronal differentiation from NG2-glia in mammals, supported by citations. They provide context for interpreting the current study's findings and suggest the mechanism may be conserved. The inference about injury-induced cues (C262) is reasonable based on the cited work.
